entries.caption: FIG. 3. (Color online) A "failed" virtual snowflake.
entries.crystalDescription: A sixfold-symmetric stellar dendrite whose six main arms carry an excessively dense thicket of sidebranches and inordinately high ridges along the arm midlines — visually snowflake-like but physically implausible, which is why the authors label it a failure.
sourceQuotes: The parameter set can be reduced, but some tuning will always be necessary, as illustrated by the "random" crystal in Fig. 3. This was obtained by choosing kappa ≡ 0.1, mu ≡ 0.001, rho = 0.1, phi = 0, and all beta's equal to 1 except beta_{01} = 1.73 and beta_{10} = beta_{20} = 1.34.

These values are in a sensible neighborhood of the parameter space, but the last attachment rates were selected by chance. The result has some physically reasonable features, but one immediately notices an excessive density of branches and inordinately high ridges.
In general, visual comparison with snow-crystal photographs is the only method we use to decide whether a virtual snowflake is a "failure" or a "success."

entries.caption: FIG. 4. (Color online) The oblique (MATLAB-rendered) and top (ray-traced) views of the crystal.
entries.crystalDescription: A six-armed stellar dendrite combining regular faceted plates with extensive sidebranching, with prominent ridges (elevations) down the middle of each main branch and fainter ridges on the sidebranches.
sourceQuotes: Our prototypical virtual snowflake has rho = 0.1 and the canonical initial state of radius 2 and thickness 1. Figure 4 depicts the crystal after 70 000 time steps, when its radius is about 350. Its parameters are beta_01 = 2.5, beta_10 = beta_20 = beta_11 = 2, beta_30 = beta_21 = beta_31 = 1, kappa ≡ 0.1, mu ≡ 0.001, and phi = 0.
These parameters reflect significant convexifying strength, pronounced, but weaker, preference for horizontal growth, and weak boundary effect.

Perhaps the most striking features shared by the virtual snowflake in Fig. 4 and physical ones are the ridges, elevations in the middle of each main branch, with less pronounced counterparts on the sidebranches.

sourceQuotes: It is perhaps surprising how dramatically this scenario depends on the initial (micrometer-scale) state. This dichotomy arises frequently in our model—within a neighborhood of the parameter space that produces planar crystals there are two stable attractors: one with outside ridges and the other a split plate with ridges on the inside.

entries.special: SUSPECTED CAPTION ERRATUM: the printed caption says rho = 0.4 (verified visually against the page image), but the surrounding text strongly indicates 0.04. V states densities are kept low to avoid the Packard regime. I transcribe the printed 0.4 as stated; do not treat it as reproduction-safe without resolving the erratum. Radius not stated for the t=120 000 capture itself (the 67-to-87 T-radius figures belong to the Fig. 12 depicted period, t=40 000 to 80 000); Z-radius grows only 6 to 7 in that period. ...it does develop fairly standard ridges that persist until about time 40 000. This is the time shown in the first frame of Fig. 12; subsequent frames show the evolution in time increments of 10 000.

entries.caption: FIG. 20. (Color online) A sandwich plate.
entries.crystalDescription: A stellar sandwich-plate crystal: six broad platelike arms with nearly featureless outer surfaces, whose main inner ridge initially connects the two plates (appearing darker in the ray-traced top view) and later splits so each plate carries its own ridge.
sourceQuotes: We now present two examples. Both start from the canonical seed and have very strong preference for horizontal growth, quite a strong convexifying tendency, and a very faint boundary layer presence.
In the first, depicted in Fig. 20, β01 = 6, β10 = β20 = 2.5, β11 = 2, and the remaining β’s are 1. All κ’s are 0.1, except that κ01 = 0.5, μ ≡ 0.0001, and ρ = 0.08.
The final radius of the crystal at the capture time 100 000 is about 150.

Note that the main ridge is interrupted: while initially it connects the two plates (and it has darker color in the ray-traced image as the background can be seen through it), it later splits and each plate has its own ridge. There is a suggestion of this phenomenon in real crystals (e.g., [8], p. 26).

entries.caption: A column capped with hexagonal plates.
entries.crystalDescription: A tsuzumi (capped column): a hexagonal hollow column carrying a large simple hexagonal plate cap at each end.
sourceQuotes: These are the tsuzumi, or capped columns, described on pp. 69-74 of [8]. They are thought to arise when crystals are transported to higher and colder regions of the atmosphere by a passing storm. Without a preferred orientation, it is most reasonable to model these as driftless.

Both our virtual snowflakes use the canonical seed and evolve with the parameters for the hollow column of Fig. 30 until time 20 000. Then they run with new parameters that promote planar growth, until time 80 000 for the first example, 60 000 for the second.

Common values for the two examples are beta_01 = 5, beta_30 = beta_21 = beta_31 = 1, kappa === 0.1, mu === 0.001, phi = 0, and rho = 0.1. The difference is the common value beta_10 = beta_20 = beta_11, which is 2.4 in Fig. 37 and 2.1 in Fig. 38. Higher attachment thresholds delay the branching instability in the first capped column so the caps are simple plates, as opposed to sectored plates in the second.

[Fig. 30 base vector, Sec. XI, p. 011601-12] The parameter set is beta_01 = 1, beta_10 = beta_20 = 2, beta_30 = beta_11 = beta_21 = 0.5, beta_31 = 1, kappa === 0.1, mu === 0.01, phi = 0, and rho = 0.1.

We remark that our virtual snowflake versions evolve in the same way. Namely, for a considerable time after the change of environment, outward growth occurs almost exclusively along the 18 edges of the hexagonal column. This is a diffusion-limited effect similar to the hollowing in Fig. 31. Then, rather suddenly, growth in the T direction takes over.

Both our virtual snowflakes use the canonical seed and evolve with the parameters for the hollow column of Fig. 30 until time 20 000. Then they run with new parameters that promote planar growth, until time 80 000 for the first example, 60 000 for the second.

Common values for the two examples are beta_01 = 5, beta_30 = beta_21 = beta_31 = 1, kappa === 0.1, mu === 0.001, phi = 0, and rho = 0.1. The difference is the common value beta_10 = beta_20 = beta_11, which is 2.4 in Fig. 37 and 2.1 in Fig. 38. Higher attachment thresholds delay the branching instability in the first capped column so the caps are simple plates, as opposed to sectored plates in the second.

[Fig. 30 base vector, Sec. XI, p. 011601-12] The parameter set is beta_01 = 1, beta_10 = beta_20 = 2, beta_30 = beta_11 = beta_21 = 0.5, beta_31 = 1, kappa === 0.1, mu === 0.01, phi = 0, and rho = 0.1.

We remark that our virtual snowflake versions evolve in the same way. Namely, for a considerable time after the change of environment, outward growth occurs almost exclusively along the 18 edges of the hexagonal column. This is a diffusion-limited effect similar to the hollowing in Fig. 31. Then, rather suddenly, growth in the T direction takes over.
entries.special: Two-stage column-to-plate environment schedule, second tsuzumi example. Stage 1 (t = 0 to 20 000) runs the hollow-column parameters of Fig. 30: beta_01 = 1, beta_10 = beta_20 = 2, beta_30 = beta_11 = beta_21 = 0.5, beta_31 = 1, kappa === 0.1, mu === 0.01, phi = 0, rho = 0.1. Stage 2 (t = 20 000 to 60 000) uses the top-level fields above with the lower beta_10 = beta_20 = beta_11 = 2.1, which lets the branching instability arrive earlier so the caps become sectored plates. Seed: the canonical seed (explicitly stated). Deliberately driftless (phi = 0, both stages). Noise epsilon never mentioned in Section XII.

entries.caption: FIG. 39. (Color online) A stellar dendrite with stunted and nucleating needles.
entries.crystalDescription: A planar six-armed stellar dendrite whose surface is dotted with symmetric rings of small bump-like protrusions resembling rime: the bumps near the center and at the tips are stunted needles, while intermediate ones have nucleated into true needles rising out of the plane.
sourceQuotes: All our final examples start from the canonical seed.

Figure 39 has features like a classic planar snowflake that has developed rime from attachment of surrounding water droplets. In fact these protrusions are potential needle instabilities—the two symmetric rings close to the center and the tips are stunted needles, whereas the intermediate needles have successfully nucleated.
The parameters of this virtual snowflake are beta_01 = 1.58, beta_10 = beta_20 = beta_11 = 1.5, beta_30 = beta_21 = beta_31 = 1, kappa == 0.1, mu == 0.006, phi = 0, and rho = 0.1.

entries.caption: FIG. 41. (Color online) A butterflake with wings in the directions of the main arms.
entries.crystalDescription: A 'butterflake': after starting as a planar crystal it nucleated large thin plates extending into the third dimension, forming butterfly-wing-like vertical blades aligned with the directions of the main arms, so the crystal looks like intersecting translucent wings rather than a flat star.
sourceQuotes: All our final examples start from the canonical seed.
The next three examples have beta == 1, mu == 0.03, kappa_10 = kappa_20 = 0.1, kappa_30 = 0.05, and kappa_11 = kappa_21 = kappa_31 = 0.01.

Our next two examples seem never to have been seen at all, and it is clear why: even if they managed to grow, their thin plates would be extremely brittle and susceptible to random fluctuations. They are characterized by very small differences in the growth rates. After starting as planar crystals, they suddenly nucleate thin structures extending into the third dimension. In Fig. 41 kappa_01 = 0.12 and rho = 0.057; in Fig. 42 kappa_01 = 0.116 and rho = 0.06.

For obvious reasons, we call these butterflakes. They are idealizations of the stellar crystals with spatial plates in [15]; chaotic snow crystals with thin plates growing every which way are relatively common.
